extracted.intended_audience: students, researchers, and practitioners of scientific method, probability, and measurement (philosophy of science and physical sciences)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for inductive inference (the inverse/Bayesian method), handling probability and coincidences, hypothesis formation/testing, and best practices for measurement and instrumentation in physical science.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule of succession (Laplace)
rubrics_metrics.description: If an event has happened m times and failed n times, the probability that it will happen on the next occasion is (m+1)/(m+n+2). When several mutually exclusive events A, B, C have been observed m, n, p times respectively (and one or other must happen), their probabilities are proportional to m+1, n+1, p+1, ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the 'm+1' adjustment (Laplace's rule of succession) to estimate probabilities from frequencies when no other information is available. The text gives numeric examples (elements: 50 metallic, 14 non-metallic → next metallic ≈ (50+1)/(64+2) etc.) and explains extension to the odds for a 'new event' (assign unity to the probability of such new event; odds: 1 for new event, m+1 for A, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Always apply the inverse (Bayesian) method when information exists
rubrics_metrics.description: We ought always to be applying the inverse method of probabilities so as to take into account all additional information; update probabilities as evidence accumulates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by the coin example: with no prior throws assume 1/2 each; after one head the chance of two heads is slightly >1/4; as more throws occur the probability for next outcome varies according to prior experience. The inverse method is 'our best and only guide' and must incorporate new data rather than rely on a priori conceptions alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-step structure of induction (hypothesis testing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Inductive reasoning is the inverse application of deduction and consists of three steps: (1) framing some hypothesis as to the general law; (2) deducing consequences from that law; (3) observing whether the consequences agree with the particular facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hypothesis must permit deductive inference to particular results that can be compared with facts. In simple cases prior familiarity may make hypothesis obvious, but where not, hypotheses must be framed and tried.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entertain and weight all conceivable hypotheses (probabilistic comparison)
rubrics_metrics.description: When deduction is only probable (not certain), we must entertain every conceivable hypothesis simultaneously and regard each with a degree of esteem proportionate to its probability of producing the observed results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform the inverse-calculus (Bayes' principle) for every conceivable hypothesis, deducing probabilities of possible consequences and comparing with facts; choose the hypothesis that most probably gives the results while retaining others with non-zero probabilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use uniform (equal) priors only as last resort
rubrics_metrics.description: When we possess no knowledge whatsoever of the conditions from which events proceed, fall back on Laplace's solution which admits, on an equal footing, every conceivable ratio of favourable and unfavourable chances for production of the event.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The uniform prior prevents over-estimating knowledge; it is 'only to be accepted in the absence of all better means' and yields general results consistent with common sense (more frequent past occurrence → more probable future recurrence, but limited longevity of such persistence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not overextend inferences beyond their data
rubrics_metrics.description: Inferences pushed far beyond their data soon lose considerable probability; no finite experience justifies saying that a law observed in the past will hold for all time to come.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: even a billion observations (sun rising) gives extremely high but not absolute probability; experience increases assurance but cannot confer certainty for unlimited future duration. Be cautious when extrapolating far beyond observed conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish casual coincidences from law-like relations
rubrics_metrics.description: No general rule can perfectly discriminate between fortuitous coincidences and effects of law; a coincidence must either be very strong in itself or corroborated by explanation or connection with other laws before being treated as law-like.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include numerical coincidences (seven vowels, seven planets) and historical coincidences; in judicial and other contexts be mindful that remarkable conjunctures of circumstances may nonetheless be due to chance. Require explanatory connection or strong corroboration before inferring causation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypotheses must be deductively testable
rubrics_metrics.description: The sole condition in framing any hypothesis is that we must have and exercise the power of inferring deductively from the hypothesis to the particular results which can be compared with known facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This makes hypothesis formation productive: only hypotheses enabling clear deductions that can be checked against data are useful for induction.

rubrics_metrics.name: When deduction is certain, empirical checks only confirm correct selection
rubrics_metrics.description: If deduction from a hypothesis yields certain consequences, comparison with facts is needed only to assure that the hypothetical conditions have been rightly selected; certainty belongs to deduction not to induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: algebraic/deductive truths are certain; no number of particular verifications adds to their certainty, whereas in empirical laws no finite number of verifications renders the law certain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measurement requires suitable instruments combined with mathematical theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Progress in physical science depends on invention of suitable instruments of measurement and the concurrent development of mathematical theory; instruments and theory should advance pari passu.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The introduction of a new instrument often marks an epoch (examples: astrolabe, telescope, pendulum, micrometer, chronometer). Precise instruments are useless without theory to anticipate and interpret results; the experimentalist must be able to compare measurements with theoretical predictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine and correct instrument errors; do not assume instruments correct
rubrics_metrics.description: An instrument should be tested for errors and observations corrected accordingly rather than assuming the instrument is correct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tycho Brahe determined the errors of his instruments and corrected his observations, which produced much greater accuracy than preceding astronomers. Always check instrument errors and atmospheric or systematic effects (e.g., refraction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Repeat observations and combine using theory of error to reduce uncertainty
rubrics_metrics.description: Extreme accuracy is achieved by multiplying observations and skilfully combining them according to the theory of error; repeating calculations/observations by different computers helps avoid mistakes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: modern reductions in observational error arise from repeated measurements and error-theory combination. However, beware that multiple independent computers can make the same systematic mistake (example: three computers made identical wrong calculations of a star's place).

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware of limits of measurement and that some phenomena remain unquantified
rubrics_metrics.description: Not all natural phenomena have been rendered measurable; some measurements may capture only a special effect rather than the full quantity (e.g., chemical action of light vs total light energy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even with instruments sensitive to millionths of units, other domains (intensity of sound, taste/smell, atomic magnitudes, temperature of electric spark) may still lack adequate measurement techniques. Recognize where measurement methods are incomplete or indirect.
